title: Muhammad
summary: Arab religious and political leader from Mecca who unified the tribes of the Arabian Peninsula under Islam, regarded by Muslims as the final prophet. His migration to Medina in 622 CE established the Islamic calendar and community.
card: Born in Mecca around 570 CE, Muhammad worked as a merchant before reporting revelations around 610 CE that form the text of the Quran. Facing opposition from the ruling Quraysh, he migrated to Yathrib (Medina) in 622 CE, an event known as the Hijra that established the Islamic lunar calendar. Over the next decade he organized the early Muslim community through diplomacy and warfare, peacefully entered Mecca in 630 CE, and died in Medina on 8 June 632 CE.
what:
Muhammad was an Arab religious, political, and military leader born in Mecca around 570 CE into the Banu Hashim clan of the Quraysh. Orphaned in early childhood, he was raised by his grandfather Abd al-Muttalib and later his uncle Abu Talib, working in caravan commerce and marrying the wealthy merchant Khadija bint Khuwaylid. Around 610 CE, during retreats in the Cave of Hira on Mount Jabal al-Nour, he reported receiving revelations from God through the angel Gabriel, calling for strict monotheism and care for the vulnerable. Muslims regard him as the final prophet and recipient of the Quran.

His public preaching met intense opposition from Meccan clan leaders whose commercial and religious prestige centered on the traditional polytheistic sanctuary of the Kaaba. In 622 CE, after years of economic boycott and escalating harassment, Muhammad and his followers emigrated northward to the oasis of Yathrib. This migration, the Hijra, established the epoch of the Islamic calendar (1 Muharram AH 1, corresponding to 16 July 622 in the Julian calendar). Renamed al-Madinah (Medina), the settlement became the capital of an expanding political commonwealth organized under the pact known as the Constitution of Medina.

Over the medinan decade, intermittent conflict with Quraysh included a major Muslim victory at Badr in 624 CE, a costly reversal at Uhud in 625 CE, and the siege of the Trench in 627 CE. Following that siege, male members of the allied Jewish tribe Banu Qurayza were condemned and executed in trenches dug in the Medina market under arbitration by Sa'd ibn Mu'adh, an episode recorded by early biographers and debated by modern historians. In 628 CE, Muhammad concluded the ten-year Treaty of al-Hudaybiyya with Quraysh, which allowed peaceful preaching across the peninsula. When Meccan allies violated the pact, Muhammad advanced on Mecca in 630 CE with an overwhelming force, entering virtually without bloodshed, granting general clemency, and removing the idols from the Kaaba. In early 632 CE he performed the Farewell Pilgrimage to Mecca, laying out ethical principles for the community. He died in Medina on 8 June 632 CE (12 Rabi al-Awwal AH 11) in the quarters of his wife Aisha. While traditional Sira narratives provide extensive biographical details, modern historians note that contemporary documentary evidence is sparse and that early Arabic literary biographies date to more than a century after his death.

uncertainty.note: Birth is traditionally placed in Mecca c. 570 CE ('Year of the Elephant'), though modern historians note an uncertainty of several years (c. 568-575 CE). Death is placed on Monday 12 Rabi al-Awwal AH 11, corresponding to 8 June 632 in the Julian calendar (11 June 632 in the proleptic Gregorian calendar); some revisionist scholars have argued for survival a few years later based on early non-Muslim sources.

how: The consolidation of Arabia under Islam proceeded through distinct ideological, political, and military phases. (1) In Mecca (c. 610–622 CE), Muhammad proclaimed monotheism, social welfare, and eschatological accountability, establishing an egalitarian core community despite clan boycotts. (2) Negotiations at al-Aqaba with representatives of the feuding Aws and Khazraj tribes of Yathrib produced mutual defense pledges, enabling the Hijra in 622 CE. (3) In Medina, the Constitution of Medina formally constituted Emigrants, local Helpers, and Jewish clans as a single political confederation (umma) under Muhammad's arbitral authority. (4) Economic conflict through caravan operations escalated into formal battles against Quraysh: the victory at Badr (624 CE) solidified Muslim prestige, while defense of the ditch during the Battle of the Trench (627 CE) broke Meccan offensive capacity. Following that siege, male members of the allied Jewish tribe Banu Qurayza were executed for treason under arbitration. (5) The Treaty of al-Hudaybiyya (628 CE) secured a ten-year truce and political recognition, facilitating diplomatic alliances with bedouin confederations across the peninsula. (6) When Meccan allies breached the truce in 630 CE, Muhammad led an army of ten thousand men into Mecca without major combat, dismantled traditional idols at the Kaaba, granted general amnesty, and accepted the submission of regional delegations during the subsequent Year of Deputations.
why_it_matters: The career of Muhammad unified the disparate and feuding pastoralist and mercantile clans of western Arabia into a single political and religious community, initiating one of the most rapid and enduring geopolitical transformations in world history. Within decades of his death in 632 CE, the nascent state based in Medina dismantled the Sasanian Persian Empire and wrested Syria, Egypt, and North Africa from Byzantine control, giving rise to an Islamic civilization whose religious, legal, linguistic, and scientific traditions came to encompass millions across three continents. Today, Islam is practiced by roughly two billion people, and the Quran revealed through him remains a foundational legal, spiritual, and literary benchmark. Had Muhammad succumbed to Meccan assassination plots during the vulnerable early years or failed to secure the migration to Yathrib in 622 CE, the polytheistic sanctuary of Mecca might have persisted as an isolated regional shrine, leaving Arabia fragmented among shifting tribal alliances under Byzantine and Sasanian peripheral influence. Without the consolidation of the Medina community, the Arab conquests that reshaped Afro-Eurasian trade, philosophy, mathematics, and urbanism would not have occurred, and world history would lack the Islamic religious and cultural synthesis that bridges classical antiquity and the modern world.

perspectives.holder: Traditional Islamic historiography (Ibn Isḥāq via Ibn Hishām, al-Wāqidī, and classical Ḥadīth collections)
perspectives.account: Maintains that the biographical tradition preserved in early compilation works faithfully reflects oral testimonies passed down through chains of transmission (isnāds) from the Prophet's immediate companions, providing a comprehensive and reliable historical chronology of Muhammad's life, political decisions, and revelatory occasions.

perspectives.holder: Historical-critical and revisionist scholarship (Patricia Crone, Michael Cook, and modern critical historians)
perspectives.account: Argues that because the earliest surviving Muslim biographical texts were written down more than a century after Muhammad's death (c. 750–800 CE), they reflect later Abbasid-era theological, sectarian, and legal concerns; therefore, historians must cross-examine traditional reports against contemporary 7th-century non-Muslim records (such as Greek and Armenian texts), early epigraphy, and physical manuscript evidence such as the Birmingham Quran folios.

perspectives.holder: Critical revisionists and traditional chroniclers on the fate of Banu Qurayza
perspectives.account: While classical biographies like Ibn Ishaq report that between 600 and 900 men of the Banu Qurayza tribe were executed following arbitration by Sa'd ibn Mu'adh, modern revisionist historians (such as W. N. Arafat) argue that these figures were exaggerated or retrofitted from earlier Jewish historical narratives, whereas traditional historians and scholars such as M. J. Kister maintain that early sources preserve the core historical reality of the arbitration and punishment under 7th-century tribal warfare customs.
